0b714b9a5968a208: SEPTEMBER 26 — The haze is back. The acrid smell of burning peat hangs in the air, skies are tinged an apocalyptic orange, and the familiar rhythm of life in Sarawak — and indeed, across Malaysia — has been disrupted. Schools close, offices slow down, and the economic machinery grinds to a halt. But this time, as we reach for our face masks, we are running out of scapegoats.

For decades, the narrative was convenient and comfortable. We blamed the smallholders. We pointed fingers at the slash-and-burn farmers in Kalimantan and Sumatra, painting them as the ecological villains of the piece. It was a tidy story: irresponsible agriculture versus responsible citizens. But the current evidence no longer supports that convenient fiction.

The fires are raging, yes. But they are raging in a landscape that has been fundamentally altered by a changing climate. The peatlands are drier than ever, the dry season is longer and more unforgiving, and the once-predictable monsoon patterns are now erratic. You cannot blame a farmer for a fire that is exacerbated by extreme drought — a drought that has its origins not in a farmer’s torch, but in the overheated machinery of our global civilisation.

Let us not kid ourselves. The smoke drifting over Borneo is not a local problem; it is a global snapshot. The EU is battling unprecedented summer infernos that consume entire towns. The US West Coast is a tinderbox, with wildfire seasons that no longer end. Australia’s bushfires have become so catastrophic that they now generate their own weather systems. We are all living in the same burning house; it is just that in this part of the world, the fire next door is blowing smoke directly into our lungs.
Thick acrid smoke from a nearby wildfire engulfs a rural stilt-supported wooden house in Ogan Ilir, South Sumatra province on September 25, 2026. — AFP pic

The economic implications of the haze are staggering. Beyond the immediate disruption to schools and offices, there is the uncalculated cost of lost productivity, the burden on healthcare systems treating respiratory illnesses, and the damage to tourism and aviation. But these are merely symptoms. The disease is our collective inertia.

We have been ignoring the evidence presented by world climate scientists for too long. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) has been issuing increasingly desperate warnings for three decades. Yet, we treat these reports as academic curiosities rather than survival manuals. We make promises at international summits, only to watch emissions rise. We set targets for 2050, while the fires burn in 2026.

This brings us to the upcoming COP31 in Turkey. If ever there was a moment to pivot from rhetoric to reality, this is it. The conference cannot simply be another carnival of pledges that will be broken by the next electoral cycle. COP31 must be the moment we accept that “appropriate measures” are not incremental tweaks to our energy policies, but a wholesale transformation of our economic system.

For the Asean region, this means we must stop viewing climate action as a “Western agenda.” The haze is our daily reminder that climate change is local. We must demand that our governments prioritise renewable energy not just for the sake of the global environment, but for the sake of our children’s ability to attend school without wearing an N95 mask. We must push for aggressive peatland restoration and moratoriums on deforestation that are actually enforced, not just announced.

But equally, we must hold the developed nations accountable. Climate justice demands that those who have emitted the most for the longest time provide the finance and technology for developing nations to leapfrog the fossil fuel era.

We are at a precipice. The haze is not just an environmental event; it is a psychological one. It induces a sense of hopelessness, a feeling that the problem is too big for any of us to solve. But despair is a luxury we cannot afford. The only antidote to the anxiety of the haze is action.

Let COP31 be the reckoning. Let it be the forum where we finally admit that the farmers are not the enemy; the enemy is our own inability to change. The world should take action, but more importantly, we should take action. Because if we wait for someone else to clear the air, we will all suffocate waiting. The time for pointing fingers is over. The time for rolling up our sleeves is now.

* Professor Datuk Dr Ahmad Ibrahim is affiliated with the Tan Sri Omar Centre for STI Policy Studies at UCSI University and is an Adjunct Professor at the Ungku Aziz Centre for Development Studies, Universiti Malaya. He can be reached at ahmadibrahim@ucsiuniversity.edu.my.

01adf4de0a3c0ad1: KEVIN Pietersen, fresh from joining England's backroom staff after over a decade away, has spoken with test coach Stephen Fleming about helping the red-ball side ahead of the next Ashes series, but said his schedule makes a broader role unlikely.

The 46-year-old Pietersen, England's third-highest run scorer across all formats, was appointed as a specialist mentor to the white-ball teams this month ahead of the 2027 one-day World Cup in southern Africa.

England host Australia in the Ashes series from June 18 to August 2, 2027, after the rivals meet in a one-off pink-ball day-night test at the Melbourne Cricket Ground in March to mark the 150th anniversary of men's test cricket.
"I've got a pretty mad schedule, (but) I wouldn't say no," Pietersen told reporters on Friday.

"I have had a conversation with Stephen but I don't think that necessarily means that I need to be in a dressing room. There's a lot of time in the lead-up to an Ashes series ... and there are conversations that can be had there.

"I've certainly had conversations with Flem about language that he would like me to use with the test batters, going into South Africa, and then certainly into the summer next year. I just don't think I can commit to a lot more time."
Pietersen also reflected on his return to the England fold more than a decade after his controversial departure from international cricket.
An explosive middle-order batter, he scored nearly 14,000 runs across all three formats for England, who last won the ODI World Cup in 2019 on home soil.

However, Pietersen's England career ended controversially in 2014 in the aftermath of the 5-0 Ashes whitewash in Australia, amid reported tensions within the dressing room and between the batsman and team management.

Pietersen was the team's top scorer in the series and, despite remaining keen to play for England, was told he was no longer part of the plans, bringing an acrimonious end to his international career.
"I'm 46, man. That stuff's so long gone. I'm a completely different person too," Pietersen said.

"I've been lucky to have worn every T-shirt an England cricketer can wear; the good, the bad and the ugly. There are parts to all of their careers which I think I could potentially help them stay away from the ugly."
In Pietersen's first series as part of the set-up, England completed a 3-0 whitewash of a spin-heavy Sri Lanka side to replace India at the top of the T20 world rankings. — REUTERS
bf79a858976de105: NEW YORK: Malaysia has called for reforms to international financial institutions and a more effective multilateral trading system for developing countries.
Foreign Minister Datuk Seri Mohamad Hasan said developing countries needed to play a meaningful role in shaping the future direction of these systems.

"Malaysia calls for reforms to international financial institutions, a more effective multilateral trading system, stronger climate action and closer cooperation in science, technology and innovation, including information and communications technology and next-generation artificial intelligence," he said.
He said this in his intervention speech at the Group of 77 and China Ministerial Meeting held in conjunction with the 81st United Nations General Assembly here today.
He also said that any reform of the UN system should strengthen its ability to meet the needs of member states, particularly developing countries.
He said Global South cooperation demonstrated that developing countries were not merely recipients of development solutions, but also strategic partners and contributors to global development.

"Malaysia's commitment to Global South cooperation is reflected through the Malaysian Technical Cooperation Programme, which supports capacity building, technical cooperation and the sharing of expertise among developing countries," he said.
Mohamad said emerging challenges such as climate change, development financing and rapid technological transformation needed to be addressed without creating new gaps to replace existing ones.
b964080fabaf60a0: ATHENS, Sept 26 — Six people, including four tourists, were missing after a building collapsed following an explosion early Friday in Athens’ historic Plaka district, which was probably caused by a huge gas leak.

The city’s mayor Haris Doukas called the blast an “unbelievable disaster” and said there was a strong possibility of an “explosion triggered by... a very significant gas leak” that led to the collapse of the two-storey building at around 7.30am (0430 GMT).
The building is just below the Acropolis.
According to police, the number of missing people rose from five to six in the evening.
“Operations are continuing, all the machinery is here, the search will go on throughout the night,” Doukas said at the scene.
“These are difficult hours. We stop whenever necessary to keep silent, so we can see if we can hear any sound” made by possible survivors, he added.

According to public television channel ERT, those missing include a Briton and a Greek woman who lived on the second floor, while four American tourists were staying in short-term rental accommodation on the first floor.
The blast on a small street shook the area, which is normally busy with hundreds of foreign visitors.
The fire service had earlier said those missing included two elderly people who lived on the building’s top floor and three tourists believed to have rented the apartment below.
Thirty firefighters were deployed with six vehicles and three search and rescue dogs, according to the Greek news agency ANA.
Excavators were clearing the rubble while rescuers used thermal cameras at the scene, according to images released by AFP.
“The damage extends along the entire street as well as the street behind the building,” the mayor said.
“We are talking about an incredible disaster,” he said, adding that two adjoining buildings were in very poor condition.
“Inspections have begun to determine whether they can remain standing or whether they too must be demolished.”
Earlier, two women were rescued from an adjacent building and taken to hospital, while another person was slightly injured by debris.
Neighbouring buildings and vehicles parked nearby were damaged.
The owner of the ground-floor apartment, Mathaios Artavanis, told the Kathimerini news outlet he had tried to contact “the elderly couple, around 70 years old” without success.

The Plaka district is one of the most touristy areas of Athens and is near Hadrian’s Arch, one of the main monuments from the Roman period in the Greek capital, where the tourist season continues to be in full swing. — AFP
495cc3a52378cd82: ALOR SETAR, Sept 26 — Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim is allowing small entrepreneurs in every village to propose aid recipients following the government’s plan to increase the specific allocation for the group in Budget 2027.
He said the suggestions were crucial to ensure the aid reaches small traders who genuinely need it and have the potential to expand their businesses.

“I want to give small traders in every village the opportunity to suggest if there are other friends who should be given a chance... because in our Budget next month, God willing, I want to increase the allocation for these entrepreneurs,” he said when officiating the Kedah Usahawan Bangkit scheme at the Federal Government Administration Complex in Anak Bukit here yesterday.
Anwar said many stalls run by small entrepreneurs also provided employment, thereby helping to generate income for the local community.
“When we give aid to these small entrepreneurs, even if it is small, they work hard and truly appreciate the assistance given,” he added.
He said the Implementation Coordination Unit (ICU) would determine the best method to assist needy small entrepreneurs after receiving the proposals.
About 1,500 entrepreneurs and petty traders in Kedah gathered at yesterday’s event to support the Madani Government’s efforts in strengthening the people’s economy.
Through the Usahawan Bangkit scheme, the government provides business equipment aid tailored to the entrepreneurs’ needs to increase their business capacity and productivity.

Meanwhile, Anwar said the government would continue to attract major foreign investments to boost the country’s economy, while ensuring the entry of foreign companies does not affect local enterprises, especially small entrepreneurs.
“Although I bring in foreign investments, I do not disrupt small entrepreneurs...I don’t go overseas for no reason,” he said.

He said investments by major companies, including in artificial intelligence (AI), computing and semiconductors, could stimulate the country’s economic growth and offer more job opportunities for the people.
Anwar also cited the development of medical technology in China, which is currently capable of treating the blind and restoring their sight.
Meanwhile, the Prime Minister stressed that the government was continuously working to alleviate the people’s burden, particularly regarding the rising cost of goods. — Bernama
109f81f969aafd40: WASHINGTON: US television networks resumed coverage of President Donald Trump's White House events on Friday, providing the first live pool access for Chinese President Xi Jinping's visit, as a legal battle continues over restrictions on CNN, MS NOW and Politico.
Trump last week banned the three outlets from the White House, before a judge ordered the administration to restore their access.

The White House television press pool aired video of Xi's arrival at the White House for tea on the final day of the Chinese leader's visit, as well as the two leaders' tour of the National Archives, which houses the US Constitution.

CNN, ABC, CBS, Fox News and NBC share the costs of covering the president and rotate coverage, providing pool footage to other outlets. The other networks' refusal to set up cameras in solidarity meant there was no pool coverage of the first two days of Xi's visit.

The Washington Post reported on Friday evening that the White House had blocked CNN from traveling with Trump on Air Force One for a trip to Tennessee, citing unnamed sources. Neither the White House nor a spokesperson at CNN immediately responded to requests for comment from Reuters.

Trump has long relied on the media to shape his public image and advance his agenda, even as he regularly casts news organizations as political adversaries. Since returning to office last year, his administration has taken an aggressive stance against major news outlets, including limiting access to the Oval Office and other restricted spaces.

As pool coverage resumed for Xi's arrival at the White House on Friday, Trump declined to answer questions from reporters on China and Iran, his media ban and a controversial new taxpayer-funded TV ad that promotes his presidency. He later thanked reporters.
"We appreciate the fair coverage. It's been very fair. We appreciate it," Trump later told reporters alongside Xi.
The White House did not respond to a request for comment about the restored press access.
UNPRECEDENTED CAMPAIGN

Trump banned the three news outlets from the White House complex over coverage he asserted was false or negative. Their access was reinstated on Thursday, after a federal judge deemed the ban likely unconstitutional and ordered their access to be immediately restored.

CNN, MS NOW and Politico sued Trump and other members of his administration, saying the ban violated the US Constitution's First Amendment protections for free speech and a free press, as well as their due process rights. A coalition of press freedom groups and dozens of news organisations, including Reuters, later filed a legal brief supporting the action.

Despite the temporary ruling restoring access, the court has not yet resolved the main challenge to the ban, based on the First Amendment of the US Constitution that protects the right to free speech and a free press. The news outlets now have until Sept 28 to ask the judge to keep their access in place while the case moves forward.
Even if the outlets won a permanent injunction against the ban, Trump could still pursue his case in federal court.

Trump has waged an unprecedented campaign against the media since returning to office last year, launching personal attacks on journalists, denying access to some outlets and suing news organisations, as well as calling on ⁠the Federal Communications Commission to strip broadcast stations of their licenses.
FRIENDLIEST PRESS CORPS

On Thursday, Trump made a joke to photographers in the Oval Office about China – which imposes strict censorship across its media – having the friendliest press corps, as he welcomed Xi to the White House.

While the White House on Thursday told the court it had reinstated CNN, MS NOW and Politico's access, CNN and MS NOW later said some of their journalists were denied access to cover Xi's arrival for the White House state dinner, according to the Washington Post.
A lawyer for the three outlets in court this week warned that the White House could again try to revoke the outlets' White House access as the current litigation continues.
David Ellison, CEO of Paramount Skydance, which is seeking to merge with CNN-parent Warner Bros. Discovery, attended the Trump-Xi state dinner Thursday night.

Critics have raised concerns about Paramount-owned CBS News tailoring coverage to favour Trump, although Ellison has promised to create an editorial independence board for both CBS and CNN as part of the deal.--REUTERS

dd66a3ffe3cd008e: KOTA KINABALU: Mother tongues risk fading when they are no longer regularly heard and spoken, particularly at home.
Kadazandusun Cultural Association president Tan Sri Joseph Pairin Kitingan said this is a risk he knew from personal experience.
Recalling his childhood, Pairin said he was separated from his parents at 10 and lived in a school hostel in Tawau, where about 90 per cent of the boarders spoke Hakka.
"So, every day I heard Hakka. Eventually, I could speak Hakka.

"But because I had no one around me speaking my mother tongue, I almost forgot it," he said when met after officiating the Borneo Cultural & Heritage Corner (BCHC) in conjunction with the Kota Kinabalu International Book Fair 2026 at the Sabah International Convention Centre here.

Pairin, the Huguan Siou or paramount leader of the Kadazandusun community, said that after becoming involved in community activities, returning to his village and visiting other districts, he began hearing local languages being spoken again.
Gradually, his command of the languages improved, and he can now speak Tambunan and Penampang, as well as some Lotud and Murut.

"Every language is at risk of disappearing over time if it is simply left alone, if nothing is done, if it is not spoken or written, especially if parents do not speak their respective languages at home.
"If there is nothing to hear, nothing goes into the mind, nothing is kept in the heart and nothing comes out in writing," he said.
He said communities needed to value the languages inherited from their ancestors and continue writing, recording and sharing them.
"Otherwise, eventually it will disappear. It will no longer be heard," he said.
At the event, Pairin also launched 25 children's books in Kadazandusun.

The books were produced through a collaboration between the Kadazandusun Language Department of Institut Pendidikan Guru (IPG) Kampus Kent, Tuaran, and the Kadazandusun Language Foundation (KLF), with the involvement of students from the Bachelor of Teaching Degree Programme (PISMP) in Kadazandusun Language under the guidance of their lecturers.
Asked whether children's books could help preserve the language, Pairin said: "I think it will definitely help."
Pairin said awareness of mother tongues was beginning to grow, including through writing, publishing and education.
"I think our awareness has begun to grow. That is why our language is now being written, published and incorporated into the school curriculum," he said.
However, he said the foundation for keeping a mother tongue alive still began at home.
"Language must be spoken at home, as the first school," he said.

f0e025ce2a54ca51: NEW MANCHESTER, Sept 26 — Kieran Canning Manchester City have been found guilty of all but one of 115 Premier League charges for breaching financial regulations, according to reports on Friday, in a ruling that will send shockwaves through English football.
No sanctions have yet been decided and it is understood the club are set to appeal.
The Premier League declined to comment when contacted by AFP over the latest developments in the case, reported first by the Athletic.
City have dominated English football for more than a decade but their reputation is on the line and they face potentially swingeing sanctions after a process that has taken two years.
The Abu Dhabi-backed club were charged by the Premier League in 2023 following an investigation into alleged breaches of rules between 2009 and 2018.
A hearing by an independent commission started in September 2024.
City were accused of failing to provide accurate financial information and details of payments to players and coaches, as well as breaches of financial sustainability rules.
They were also charged with failing to cooperate with an investigation.
The club strongly denied all charges at the time and said their case was supported by a “comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence”.
A club spokesperson said Friday that their position had not changed.

“The Premier League process remains ongoing, with significant elements to be completed, and subject to strict confidentiality. As such, Manchester City FC’s position remains consistent with the club’s statement of February 2023.

“The club has diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that the Premier League board and executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence.”
Severe sanctions expected
German outlet Der Spiegel published leaked documents including emails purportedly sent between top City executives in 2018.

It alleged the documents showed the club had inflated sponsorship revenue from Abu Dhabi state-controlled airline Etihad and telecoms firm Etisalat by disguising direct investment from Sheikh Mansour’s Abu Dhabi United Group as income.
Other documents purportedly showed off-the-books payments to former manager Roberto Mancini via consultancy fees from a club in Abu Dhabi.
In 2020, Uefa imposed a two-year European ban on City as well as a fine for breaking financial fair-play rules, though that ban was later overturned by the Court of Arbitration for Sport.
If the club are found guilty, sanctions could include a severe points deduction and possibly even expulsion from the Premier League.
Everton and Nottingham Forest were both hit by points deductions in the 2023/24 season for single breaches of profit and sustainability rules.
A severe punishment would also raise doubts over the future of City’s cast of star players, including prolific striker Erling Haaland.
Other clubs could make a claim for titles to be stripped and for compensation.
“Another Premier League medal to be added to the cabinet,” posted former Manchester United defender Rio Ferdinand, who was part of the United team to finish second to City in the 2011/12 season.
But British Prime Minister Andy Burnham warned people should not “jump to conclusions” on City, when asked whether they should be stripped of their Premier League titles.
“I think we would all need to study the independent commission’s report in some considerable detail before reaching any conclusions,” he told ITV Granada Reports.
Spain’s World Cup-winning captain Rodri, who left City for Barcelona last month, said: “I believe in the justice system and I believe in the innocence of the club.”
Under the ownership of Sheikh Mansour, whose Abu Dhabi United Group acquired the club in 2008, City have become the dominant force in English football.
They have won eight Premier League titles, a Champions League crown and multiple other trophies over the past 15 years.
The latest developments in the case come just months after Pep Guardiola left the club after a golden decade.
Guardiola always backed the club’s stance on the charges but threatened to walk away if he felt he had been lied to and they were proven to be true.
Despite Guardiola’s departure, City are top of the Premier League after a perfect start under new boss Enzo Maresca.
The Italian has been backed by an outlay of about £460 million (RM2.48 billion; US$608 million (RM2.48 billion)) on new players including Enzo Fernandez, Elliot Anderson and Ayyoub Bouaddi. — AFP

20e9d92eba49e3fa: KUALA LUMPUR, Sept 26 — A 14-year-old Form Two student died last night after being found unconscious at a school hostel in Kuala Pilah, Negeri Sembilan, amid allegations from his family that he had been bullied.
Kuala Pilah district police chief Superintendent Muhamad Mustafah Hussin confirmed the incident and said further details would be released soon, the New Straits Times reported.

His body was subsequently transferred to the Forensic Medicine Department at Tuanku Ja’afar Hospital in Seremban for a post-mortem examination.
Berita Harian reported separately that a woman claiming to be the boy’s aunt had posted about his death on Threads last night, alleging that he had been assaulted while at the school hostel.
The woman said she learnt of her nephew’s death after receiving a call from her younger sister, who is the boy’s mother.
“Angah called me earlier, crying, saying her son had died after being beaten at the school hostel.
“Everyone is now on the way to Kuala Pilah Hospital,” she wrote, according to Berita Harian.
In a subsequent post, the woman said the boy’s body had initially been at Kuala Pilah Hospital before being transferred to Seremban for a post-mortem.
She also alleged that a Form Four student had been detained in connection with the case.
Police have not publicly confirmed the alleged detention.
In another post this morning, the woman said the post-mortem examination was scheduled for noon.

Black sesame seeds have a pronounced nutty aroma — Picture by CK Lim
Here is where the little details make a difference.
Black sesame is the base, providing the characteristic deep, almost ink-black colour as well as the more robust flavour we associate with sesame paste.
It has a pronounced nutty aroma with a toasted, earthy character. On its own, however, it can sometimes make the finished paste taste a little heavy or one-dimensional.
This is where white sesame comes in. Its higher fat content and thinner outer skin allow it to release plenty of fragrant oil when toasted.
Rather than overpowering the black sesame, it helps develop its aroma further, while contributing to a smoother and more luxurious texture. The result is a paste.
What we get as a result tastes richer and less bitter, while retaining some of that characteristic stickiness that makes a good bowl of sesame paste so enjoyable.
Double black and white ‘tong sui’

The first step is to stir-fry the sesame seeds until fragrant before grinding everything into a fine paste and cooking it. It may sound like an extra bit of work, but this is what helps bring out the aroma of the sesame and gives the finished paste a fuller, more rounded flavour.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Stir-fry the sesame seeds, stirring regularly to ensure they toast evenly — Picture by CK Lim

When it comes to the sesame seeds, I find that a ratio of about 3:1 for black sesame to white sesame works particularly well. Black sesame remains the star of the show, while the smaller amount of white sesame helps to round out its flavour and texture.
There is also a visual reason for keeping the proportion of white sesame relatively low. Part of the appeal of black sesame paste is its beautiful, glossy, ink-like colour.

Use too much white sesame and the finished paste starts to look grey and pale instead of the deep black we are after. A 1:1 ratio, for instance, would give you plenty of white sesame flavour but would sacrifice much of that familiar appearance.
So, think of the white sesame as a supporting player rather than an equal partner. It is there to lift the aroma and texture while allowing the black sesame to remain firmly in the spotlight.
The rice is another small change that makes quite a noticeable difference.
Traditionally, white rice is used to create the slurry for sesame paste. In this recipe I replace half of the white rice with black glutinous rice.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Use black glutinous rice alongside the traditional white rice to create the slurry — Picture by CK Lim
Apart from giving the paste an even deeper colour, black glutinous rice contributes a pleasant chewiness and also contains anthocyanins, adding another nutritional benefit.
This is why I call this particular recipe “Double Black & White Tong Sui” rather than just the singular version; we have black sesame and black glutinous rice as well as white sesame and white rice.

There is, of course, some room to adjust things according to your own preference. A little more black sesame will give you a stronger, more assertive flavour, while increasing the white sesame will make the paste more fragrant and mellow.
After all, some people like their sesame paste thick and almost oozing from the spoon. Others prefer it looser and more fluid, closer to a traditional Cantonese tong sui.
Both are perfect, so long as it is perfect for you.
Ingredients
100g black sesame seeds
30g white sesame seeds
15g black glutinous rice
15g white rice
800ml water
50g rock sugar or slab sugar, adjusted to taste
Coconut milk, for finishing (optional)
Method
Combine the black and white sesame seeds. Wash and drain thoroughly.

Dry-roast the sesame seeds in a wok or pan over low heat, stirring regularly to ensure they toast evenly. Continue for about 5 minutes, or until they become fragrant. Remove from the heat and set aside to cool.
Lightly dry-roast the black glutinous rice and white rice, if desired, until they become aromatic. Remove from the heat and allow them to cool.
Transfer the toasted sesame seeds and rice to a bowl. Add a small amount of water and soak for about 30 minutes. Here the rice acts as a starch slurry to thicken the sesame paste.
Pour the soaked sesame seeds, rice and soaking water into a blender. Blend thoroughly until you have a very fine, smooth mixture.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Blend everything together before cooking — Picture by CK Lim
Add the remaining water and sugar to a pot. Heat over medium heat, stirring until the sugar has completely dissolved.
Pour the blended sesame mixture into the pot. Bring the mixture to a gentle simmer, then reduce the heat to low.

Stir continuously as the mixture cooks to prevent it from catching on the bottom of the pot. Continue simmering for 5–10 minutes, or until the sesame paste has thickened to a smooth, creamy consistency.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
‘Double Black & White Tong Sui’ for two — Picture by CK Lim
Serve warm, drizzled with some coconut milk, if desired.

c531fe043026586f: AFTER the United States was walloped 5-0 in Friday's five foursomes at the Presidents Cup, captain Brandt Snedeker is relying on a mix of old and new to start Saturday off right.

Scottie Scheffler and Sam Burns will head out together for the third time in as many sessions, but for the first time they will play in the anchor match instead of the opener in morning four-ball at Medinah Country Club outside Chicago.
Their opponents on the International team – which leads the competition 7-3 in a surprising turn – will be Japan's Hideki Matsuyama and Ryo Hisatsune.

Justin Thomas and Jackson Koivun will play in the opening match against Australia's Min Woo Lee and South Korea's Sungjae Im. The Korean pairing of Si Woo Kim and Tom Kim will stay together for the third consecutive session and go up against Collin Morikawa and Wyndham Clark. And Chris Gotterup and Cameron Young will take on Canadians Nick Taylor and Corey Conners before the Scheffler/Burns tandem tees off last.

Of the four American pairings, three of them won a point on Thursday in the initial four-ball (best-ball) session. The only new combination is the long drivers Gotterup and Young, neither of whom have collected a point so far.
Snedeker conceded at his press conference that the US had to "look at" its game plan.

"We've got a lot of high-character guys in our room," the first-time captain said. "I love the way the guys competed today. It's a long golf tournament. I keep telling those guys this is a football game and we're not even at halftime yet. We've got three more sessions to go, a lot of golf in front of us. I'm really confident in our guys. I'm really confident in what they bring to the table. I'm excited about this challenge."
Scheffler and Burns beat Lee and Im 1 up on Thursday before Conners and Taylor struck back Friday with a 1-up win over the tandem.

Matsuyama and Hisatsune reunite for the International side after they scored their team's first point with a 3-and-1 win over Young and Xander Schauffele. The Kim/Kim pairing is the hottest one going, having defeated Gotterup and Patrick Cantlay 3 and 2 on Thursday and Cantlay/Schauffele 4 and 3 in a Friday foursomes rout.
Sitting out the Saturday morning session for the US are Cantlay, Schauffele, Russell Henley and Jacob Bridgeman.

b84bf16eaa392924: KUALA LUMPUR, Sept 26 — Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim described his recent working visit to Shanghai and Hangzhou as yielding significant results, particularly in harnessing investment potential and trade cooperation that will generate widespread benefits and prosperity for both Malaysia and China.

892fd8e8b59feab8: WASHINGTON: TikTok on Friday agreed to pay Alabama at least US$100 million and enact limits for teen users, avoiding a trial set to begin next week in the southern US state over claims related to child safety on the platform.

"Under the settlement, Alabama will receive a minimum of US$100 million, due to the state within 45 days, with the potential to receive up to US$300 million if certain conditions are met," the office of the Attorney General Steve Marshall said.
The trial had been set to begin on Monday with jury selection.
According to Marshall, TikTok has agreed to enact two-hour daily time limits and restrict access for children from midnight to 6am, among a host of other parental and other safety features.
Alabama's suit was the latest in a wave of litigation targeting social media companies across the United States over the harm their apps allegedly cause young users.
TikTok had also previously settled cases against it that were headed for trial, including a Los Angeles lawsuit brought by a young woman and a suit from a Kentucky school district.
Meta, by contrast, has taken its chances in court – with bruising results.
In March, a jury in New Mexico ordered the Facebook and Instagram owner to pay US$375 million after finding it had misled the public about the safety of its platforms for children.
That same month, a Los Angeles jury found Meta and Google's YouTube negligent in the case of a 20-year-old woman who said she became hooked on social media as a child, awarding her US$6 million.
In August, Meta agreed to pay US$18 billion to settle a sweeping lawsuit brought by US states accusing it of designing Instagram and Facebook to addict children.
Going to trial would have exposed TikTok to unprecedented public scrutiny of how it handles safety internally, with company documents and executive testimony potentially aired in open court.
Alabama originally sued TikTok and its Chinese parent company ByteDance in April 2025, alleging the app was engineered to hook young users "just like a sophisticated gambling machine."

The state later narrowed its case to claims under Alabama's Deceptive Trade Practices Act, focusing on whether TikTok misrepresented the effectiveness of features such as "Restricted Mode" and "Kids Mode."
In its complaint, the state said investigators set up TikTok accounts posing as 13-, 14- and 15-year-olds in Alabama and switched on Restricted Mode.

Despite TikTok's assurances that users in that mode should not see mature themes, the accounts were quickly served videos about suicide, self-harm, eating disorders, alcohol and sex, according to the filing.
The state also accused TikTok of falsely telling app stores the platform was suitable for children aged 12 and up and contained only mild or infrequent mature content.

TikTok, whose US operations were transferred this year to a venture led by American investors, has argued that the case should be paused and that it is shielded by Section 230, a federal law that protects online platforms from liability for content posted by users.

Asked for comment on the settlement Friday, a TikTok spokesperson said the company's "priority has always been fostering a safe and positive space where people can be creative, discover what they love, and connect with their community."
"This builds on our commitment and core objective to continually enhance our robust safety tools to protect teens," the spokesperson added.--AFP

2f619f768214dcfd: NEW YORK, Sept 26 — Wall Street stocks bounced Friday to finish a volatile week on a positive note, greeting a drop in oil prices on hopes for a US-Iran agreement that could lead to the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz.

a553289d7be9e887: SEPTEMBER 26 — Article 37(1) of the Negeri Sembilan State Constitution (Undang-Undang Tubuh Kerajaan Negeri Sembilan – UUTKNS) mandates the establishment of the offices of State Secretary, State Legal Adviser and State Financial Officer,
The appointments to the offices “shall be made by the appropriate Service Commission from amongst members of any of the relevant public services”.

The “appropriate Service Commission” for the State Legal Adviser is the Judicial and Legal Service Commission (JLSC) established under Article 138 of the Federal Constitution. By Clause (2) of the Article, the Attorney General is a member of the JLSC.
State Legal Advisers report to, and take instructions from, the AG.
The State Legal Adviser for Negeri Sembilan advises on legal matters referred to him by His Highness or the state government.
“His Highness” refers to the Yang di-Pertuan Besar.
A general view of the Negeri Sembilan State Legislative Assembly building in Seremban on April 23, 2026. — Picture by Yusof Isa
So, how does the AG stay out of state affairs of Negeri Sembilan as urged by the four undangs?

Article 71 of the Federal Constitution guarantees the right of a Ruler of a State to succeed and to hold, enjoy and exercise the constitutional rights and privileges of the Ruler of that State in accordance with the Constitution of that State.
However, any dispute as to the title to the succession as Ruler of any State “shall be determined solely by such authorities and in such manner as may be provided by the Constitution of that State”.

There is clearly a dispute as to the title to the succession as Ruler of Negeri Sembilan which requires determination not only by “such authorities” but also “in the manner as may be provided” by the UUTKNS.
The views and opinions expressed are not about interfering with, and intervening in, the State’s affairs.
It’s just about the plain readings of the federal and state constitutions.

0093d838579d68c2: SEPTEMBER 26 — A friend shared with me a New Straits Times report on Sultan Nazrin Muizzuddin Shah’s remarks about the history of Universiti Malaya (UM), and the headline immediately caught my eye: “UM’s intellectual freedom eroded after May 1969, says Sultan Nazrin.”
I was glad to see it stated so plainly, because it speaks to a concern that Malaysian higher education has too often been reluctant to confront directly.

Reflecting on UM’s development alongside Malaysia’s broader political and social transformation, Sultan Nazrin pointed to the effects of the New Economic Policy (NEP) on the student body and language of instruction, the curtailment of political freedom of expression, and the erosion of the vibrant intellectual and political discourse that had characterised the university’s earlier years.

His remarks reach beyond the history of one university. They invite a wider examination of how Malaysian universities developed their relationship with political authority, and how caution became embedded in decisions over what can be discussed, who can be invited and which controversies institutions are prepared to accommodate.
At the heart of this discussion is intellectual freedom itself. Universities exist to create, examine, contest and transmit knowledge.
That function requires space in which arguments can be pursued without having to conform to prescribed doctrine or prevailing political positions.
The idea that intellectual freedom belongs to the foundation of the university long predates contemporary debates over academic freedom.

In 1810, Wilhelm von Humboldt argued that freedom was one of the governing principles of the university and that intellectual work could flourish only when scholars were allowed to pursue knowledge without external direction.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

The author argues that repealing UUCA will mean little unless Malaysian universities also dismantle the administrative habits and self-censorship that continue to restrict intellectual freedom. — Picture by Miera Zulyana
He also recognised that constraints on freedom could arise from universities themselves, a warning that remains strikingly relevant today.
This is also why the period after May 1969 should not be compressed into a simple account of campuses falling silent.
Student politics remained active across Malaysian institutions into the early 1970s, with UM as one important centre among several.
Students organised around socialist, nationalist, Islamic and language-based currents and engaged with poverty, inequality, language, foreign policy and the direction of the postcolonial state.
Mobilisation continued into 1974 through struggles including Tasik Utara in Johor Bahru and the protests surrounding poverty and declining incomes among rural communities in Baling.
The December demonstrations led to mass arrests and the detention of student leaders, academics and activists.
Campus politics remained very much alive after May 1969, even as the political environment around it was becoming more restrictive.
The Universities and University Colleges Act 1971 (UUCA) established a new framework for higher education during this period of institutional expansion.
The more restrictive 1975 amendments, following the mobilisations of 1974, imposed much tighter limits on political organisation and participation.

Their significance extended beyond the legal provisions themselves. Political participation increasingly became something to be supervised through rules governing organisations, events and activities, while university administrations acquired greater authority over permissible forms of expression.
The law institutionalised habits of governance that outlasted the political circumstances that produced them.
That history is important because restrictions on intellectual freedom rarely operate through law alone.
They also take shape through institutional routines, approval structures and assumptions about what a university should permit.
Malaysia has amended the UUCA several times, experienced changes of government and spoken increasingly about autonomy and academic freedom.
Yet controversy still tends to trigger demands for greater control, now expressed through the language of security, sensitivities, reputation, background checks and compliance.
The difficulty arises when these considerations are interpreted so broadly that intellectual disagreement itself begins to be treated as a risk.

Several examples give substance to that concern. Fahmi Reza’s Student Power lectures on the history of Malaysian student activism encountered restrictions at UM beginning 2009 and at Universiti Teknologi MARA (UiTM) in 2010.
In October 2014, UM refused approval for then Opposition leader Anwar Ibrahim to address an event organised by students.

The programme proceeded amid a campus lockdown, and student leader Fahmi Zainol was subsequently suspended for two semesters and fined RM600, although the disciplinary decision was later quashed by the courts on procedural grounds.

The restrictions persisted across subsequent political transitions. In 2018, Hishamuddin Rais said he was prevented from speaking at Universiti Kebangsaan Malaysia (UKM) at a discussion on contemporary Malaysian politics.
During Fahmi Reza’s 2022 Kelas Demokrasi tour ahead of GE15, he was barred from entering or prevented from continuing sessions at several public universities.

At UM in 2025, students said a forum examining whether Malaysia should be understood as a secular or religious state was cancelled because it touched on race, religion and royalty, while student organisers said another programme on assembly rights was stopped on security and public order grounds.
These cases span different governments and university administrations, which makes them harder to dismiss as the preferences of any single administration.
The Bruce Gilley controversy at UM in April 2024 brought this tension into especially clear view.

His remarks attracted extensive criticism, after which the Higher Education Ministry ordered the cancellation of his remaining programmes, asked UM to investigate and reminded universities to conduct background checks on invited speakers, take societal sensitivities into account and align decisions with government policies and positions.

Zambry Abd Kadir later said that universities did not require ministry approval to invite international speakers and that their freedom should be respected, while also maintaining that invited experts should not contradict important Malaysian positions.

The issue, however, extends beyond any one speaker. Controversial arguments and public records should remain open to rigorous scrutiny, and universities should preserve the intellectual space in which that scrutiny can take place rather than remove the possibility in advance.
The concern becomes more serious when the acceptability of an academic programme begins to depend on conformity with government positions or administratively defined institutional positions.
Universities need sufficient intellectual independence to examine, support or challenge prevailing positions according to evidence and scholarship.
When conformity becomes an implicit condition of legitimate inquiry, intellectual freedom and institutional autonomy are compromised at their core.

Background checks require the same distinction. Reasonable due diligence may consider expertise, professional standing, the academic purpose of an event, credible safety concerns and relevant legal obligations.
Universities are also entitled to uphold institutional principles and ethical standards. Intellectual freedom does not require academic institutions to suspend judgment or abandon their values.
Yet values and principles have to be applied with intellectual precision. They cannot become undefined categories through which controversial or politically inconvenient positions are screened out.
A university should be capable of explaining why a proposed event lacks academic merit, violates a clearly stated institutional principle or creates a genuine legal or safety problem.
“Controversial”, “sensitive” and “likely to attract criticism” are much weaker grounds.
When these become sufficient reasons for intervention, intellectual boundaries begin to be determined administratively rather than academically.
The recent controversy at IIUM involving Abdul Razak Baginda illustrates why that distinction is so important.
The university cancelled a proposed public lecture on leadership after the invitation attracted criticism given Razak’s public and legal history.

IIUM’s Academic Staff Association had raised serious concerns, yet it did not simply demand that the event be prohibited. If the lecture proceeded, the association suggested bringing in another speaker or discussant to provide a contrasting perspective, allowing the moderator to raise questions directly related to Razak’s public history and structuring the event to encourage critical engagement.
It argued that these measures could strengthen the academic integrity of the programme.

Upholding intellectual freedom means protecting the space in which difficult ideas can be examined seriously, while recognising that universities still have a responsibility to exercise academic judgment.
Who is invited, for what purpose and with what intellectual contribution should matter.
An invitation should never be treated casually, but neither should it automatically be read as endorsement of everything a speaker has said, done or represented.

A controversial figure may be invited precisely because their arguments or public role deserve scrutiny, and the university should create the conditions for those arguments to be challenged rigorously.
Academics must be able to judge intellectual relevance, frame difficult discussions, test claims and provide context, while students must remain free to question, criticise and reject what they hear.
Legal and genuine safety concerns remain legitimate, but administrative risk management should not determine the boundaries of intellectual inquiry.
Intellectual freedom does not remove judgment; it requires that such judgment remain grounded in academic purpose rather than political comfort.
The connection with the 1970s lies here. The mechanisms are no longer identical, and contemporary Malaysian universities operate in a very different environment.
They are larger, more bureaucratic, more exposed to rankings and markets, and increasingly attentive to reputational management.
Formal regulation now exists alongside event approvals, speaker vetting, risk assessments and multiple layers of institutional procedure. Control can therefore operate quietly.
Academics and students learn which invitations will generate difficulty, which subjects require additional approval and which controversies are safer to avoid.
By the time self-censorship takes hold, direct prohibition becomes almost unnecessary.
The planned repeal of the UUCA gives Malaysia an opportunity to rethink more than the law itself.
In August 2026, the government announced its intention to repeal the Act and develop a new higher education legal framework.

Yet laws can change more quickly than institutional cultures. Intellectual freedom also depends on preserving a clear distinction between academic judgment and political or administrative convenience.

Decisions over intellectual programmes should rest on academic purpose, scholarly standards, institutional principles, legal obligations and genuine safety concerns, rather than political embarrassment or anticipated outrage.

Sultan Nazrin’s remarks bring this longer trajectory back into view. The restrictions that followed May 1969 took shape during a period of political instability, nation-building and intense student activism, but many of the controls and habits introduced then endured even as Malaysia changed.
More than 50 years later, restrictions on intellectual freedom do not always come through an explicit ban.
They can also take shape through ordinary procedures, approvals and administrative decisions that appear routine on their own.
Intellectual freedom is foundational to the university. Knowledge cannot advance when inquiry must first satisfy political, ideological or reputational expectations.
Universities must protect the space in which ideas can be tested seriously, including those that unsettle orthodoxies, challenge powerful institutions and make people uncomfortable.
The coming reform of Malaysian higher education should therefore be judged by whether our universities can defend that intellectual independence when it is most difficult to do so.
If they cannot, then what exactly are they protecting, and what becomes of the university itself?
* Khoo Ying Hooi, PhD is an associate professor at Universiti Malaya.

8958b64c7a615ada: UNITED NATIONS (New York), Sept 26 — Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Friday that Tehran had offered Washington a plan that would see the Strait of Hormuz reopened to maritime navigation within seven days once agreed.
Araghchi met for talks on Tuesday with US President Donald Trump’s envoy Steve Witkoff, and previously set out conditions for ending the war and reopening the vital energy shipping channel.

“Iran has conveyed to the United States, through Qatar, a concrete seven-day plan. If the necessary conditions are met, the strait can be reopened, and normal maritime passage restored within seven days,” Araghchi said at the UN Friday.
“The choice now rests with the United States. Iran does not accept coercion, threats, or intimidation, and Iran will not surrender its sovereign rights under pressure.
“I can tell you if there is seriousness in the US side to come to a deal and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, everything is now prepared.”
Earlier media reports suggest the new plan calls for a cessation of all hostilities in the Middle East for seven days, including in Lebanon.

It also reportedly calls for the release of frozen Iranian assets estimated to be worth at least $12 billion, as well as the lifting of sanctions on Iranian oil and an end to the US naval blockade of Iran.
On the seventh day of the truce, Iran would reopen Hormuz.

Hossein Mohebi, a spokesman for the Revolutionary Guards, the ideological arm of Iran’s military, told AFP in an exclusive interview on Tuesday that ending hostilities in Yemen was also among Tehran’s demands.
The US and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding in June that aimed to end the war, reopen the strait and launch talks on Iran’s nuclear programme.
But the deal broke down shortly afterward when Iran fired on commercial ships in Hormuz that it accused of deviating from its approved route through the waterway.
Iran requires ships to obtain authorisation before passage, citing security and sovereignty reasons.
Ships that refuse to comply are regularly targeted, while the United States sporadically bombs Iranian coastal areas in retaliation. — AFP

8f08b983e2a5a3bf: SEPTEMBER 26 — In a beautiful and eloquent description of the Conference of Rulers, the country’s leading expert of constitutional law, Professor Dr Shad Faruqi wrote as follows:

“The mystique of the monarchy is best reflected in the unique institution of the Conference of Rulers. This august assembly dates back to July 1897 when it met for the first time in Kuala Kangsar, the citadel of the Sultan of Perak.

“Under the Federal Constitution, the Conference of Rulers has been invested with a number of critical constitutional functions, including veto power over some constitutional amendments, right to be consulted on some key government appointments and right to deliberate on national policies, including matters relating to Islam and Malay privileges.
“The conference has the great constitutional role of electing the Yang di-Pertuan Agong and the Timbalan Yang di-Pertuan Agong. It has the dramatic power to dismiss the King.

“If the King or a ruler is to be tried in a court under Article 182, the conference has the authority to appoint two out of the five judges on the Special Court. If the King or a Sultan or the consort of the King or a Sultan is found guilty in a court, the conference has the power to grant a pardon, reprieve, respite, remission, suspension or commutation of the sentence.”
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

File photo of the Negeri Sembilan Dewan Keadilan dan Undang. The author argues that disputes over succession to the Negeri Sembilan rulership must be determined under the state constitution, not by the Conference of Rulers. — Bernama pic
The eminent Dr Shad then went on to explain the constitutional functions of the Conference of Rulers as are set out by Article 38(2) of the Federal Constitution, that is, on:
election and dismissal of the Yang di-Pertuan Agong;
legislative veto of federal legislation on several critical and sensitive issues such as the privileges, position, honours or dignities of the Rulers and alteration of the boundaries of a state;
appointments of several critical federal posts such as judges of the superior courts, Auditor–General, and chairpersons and members of the Public Services Commission and the Election Commission;
extension of any religious acts to the Federation as a whole;
changes in policy relating to privileges of the Malays and the natives of Sabah and Sarawak;
pardon;
Special Court; and
national policy.
Not listed above is succession as a ruler of a state.
Behold, Article 71 of the Federal Constitution guarantees the State Constitutions.

Under Clause (1), the Federation “shall guarantee the right of a Ruler of a State to succeed and to hold, enjoy and exercise the constitutional rights and privileges of Ruler of that State in accordance with the Constitution of that State; but any dispute as to the title to the succession as Ruler of any State shall be determined solely by such authorities and in such manner as may be provided by the Constitution of that State”. (Emphasis added)
Under Clause (2), the guarantee in Clause (1) extends “with the necessary modifications” to a Ruling Chief of Negeri Sembilan.

In other words, while the federal guarantee extends to a Ruling Chief, any dispute as to the succession as the State Ruler shall be determined solely by such authorities and in such manner as may be provided by the State Constitution – that is, the Undang-Undang Tubuh Kerajaan Negeri Sembilan (UUTKNS).

Accordingly, and with due respect, a notification to the Conference of Rulers of Tunku Nadzaruddin Tuanku Ja’afar’s selection as the State’s 12th Yang di-Pertuan Besar and therefore the only person with lawful authority to perform the functions of the Yang di-Pertuan Besar under the UUTKNS, including attending meetings of the Conference of Rulers, does not determine the succession to rulership of the State.
It is not a constitutional function of the Conference of Rulers to determine who between Tuanku Muhriz and Tunku Nadzruddin is the Yang di-Pertuan Besar.

9715138721187862: SEPTEMBER 26 — I’ve never been much of a gamer. While die-hard video game purists spent decades complaining about fidelity to source material and whether this or that is canon or not, I’ve always approached video game adaptations from a purely cinematic perspective.
And as a film fan, I think it’s safe to say that I am one of those rare people who actually loved the original Resident Evil film franchise spearheaded by Paul W.S. Anderson.
Love might even be too light a word to be used as I can be found guilty of singing his praises for what must have been more than a decade, on every platform imaginable.

Why? Well, and here I go again with my championing of Anderson’s Resident Evil movies, for all the critical snobbery aimed at those movies, Anderson’s six-film cycle possessed genuine artistic merits and high-minded visual ambitions.

More specifically, his work fits squarely into the realm of “expressive esoterica,” a concept famously coined by film critic Andrew Sarris to describe cinema that prioritises formal visual abstraction and smart editing rhythms over traditional narrative mechanics.
Entries like Resident Evil: Afterlife and Resident Evil: Retribution are particularly breathtaking in this regard.

Anderson crafted some of the most beautiful, purely formalist uses of CGI and slow-motion photography ever produced within a major Hollywood studio in these films, turning pulp action into mesmerising, avant-garde digital ballet.
So, walking into this latest cinematic reboot, I knew things were going to be radically different.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

The author argues that Zach Cregger’s ‘Resident Evil’ succeeds by combining claustrophobic horror, dark humour and video-game-inspired POV filmmaking into a confident new direction for the franchise. — Picture courtesy of Sony Pictures
With director Zach Cregger taking the reins, I was more than prepared for a complete pivot in style, and that was fine by me.

Having been thoroughly impressed by Cregger’s work on Barbarian and Weapons, I was eager to see how his distinct directorial voice would handle the umbrella of biological horror, pun absolutely intended.
Cregger takes this new Resident Evil in a far more straightforward narrative direction than Anderson’s surreal, dream logic aesthetics.
Rather than assembling a tactical ensemble team, the film stays relentlessly anchored to its single main protagonist, Bryan Hodukavich (brilliantly played by Austin Abrams, who was also in Weapons).
By keeping the narrative strictly centred on Bryan’s lone journey through the nightmare-riddled town of Raccoon City, Cregger turns the film into a claustrophobic character study of survival.
Abrams brings a frantic, deeply sympathetic vulnerability to Bryan, making his every move through the sprawling labyrinth feel terrifyingly immediate.

Instead of sprawling, sterile glass corridors and hyper-stylised digital trickery, Cregger places an absolute premium on brilliantly executed suspense set-pieces that build dread through meticulous spatial awareness and exquisite timing.
What makes the film glide so effortlessly, however, is Cregger’s by-now trademark injection of humour into the proceedings.
Just when the claustrophobia threatens to become suffocating, Cregger drops in moments of pitch-black, situational comedy through Bryan’s bewildered reactions.

It releases the pressure without ever undercutting the genuine threat of the biological horrors lurking in the dark, keeping the narrative momentum going and the audience thoroughly entertained throughout its runtime.
Yet, despite taking a more straightforward narrative route, Cregger hasn’t completely abandoned video game grammar.
There are many parts of the movie where the POV camera style makes it feel as if we’re playing the game ourselves, which is helped immensely by the film’s sole focus on Bryan.

By making Bryan our point of entry into the film, the audience not only assumes Bryan’s point of view, but also kind of becomes a player in this Resident Evil video game, thanks to the passages in the film where the POV camera style takes over.
This subjective visual approach immediately recalls that of another brilliant video game adaptation, the Japanese film Exit 8, which was on my list of favourite genre films last year.

Much like how Exit 8 used a tight, claustrophobic POV to trap the viewer inside an endless, uncanny subway corridor, Cregger uses this perspective to heighten the audience’s disorientation and vulnerability.
We are forced to look down narrow, unlit hallways through Bryan’s flashlight beam, where every turn of the camera carries an agonising sense of anticipation.
Ultimately, this new entry proves that Cregger is no one hit wonder. It firmly cements his reputation as modern horror’s brightest new star director.

His rapid, uncompromising rise in the industry directly mirrors that of Jordan Peele (of Get Out, Us and Nope fame), a filmmaker who transitioned seamlessly from comedy roots into crafting masterclasses in contemporary horror.

Cregger understands that horror works best when the director respects the craft of the set-piece, and with Resident Evil, he delivers a tense, thrilling, and supremely confident ride that marks an exciting new chapter for the franchise.
* This is the personal opinion of the columnist.
322a56ec9d520f28: PENDANG: Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim has denied trying to interfere in the Negri Sembilan royal crisis.
He said he was defending the constitutional monarchy system practised in the country.
Anwar said he did not want action by the Undangs in the state to remove the Yang di-Pertuan Besar too easily, as this could lead to a wider crisis for the constitutional monarchy system.

He said the Negri Sembilan laws stipulated that a change could only be made on specific grounds, including if the Yang di-Pertuan Besar became mentally incapacitated, lost his sight or speech, became disqualified under Islamic law, committed an act detrimental to the dignity of the office or deliberately disregarded the state constitution.
"That is why the Attorney-General took a firm decision that we cannot make it easy to remove a ruler.

"Imagine if this starts there. Tomorrow, the prime minister and cabinet might think they want to replace the Yang di-Pertuan Agong, and write to the Malay rulers saying they do not agree with the Agong.

"That cannot be done. It is not the prime minister's power to decide to replace the Agong. The prime minister is the chief executive who administers the country and there are limits to his powers. He cannot amend the Constitution on matters concerning Islam, the Malay language, Malay special rights and the institution of the rulers," he said.
He said this when speaking at the Sebarkan Salam and Pendang Berselawat programme at Pondok Mujamma' Ibn Sunni Al-Talaqqi here last night.
Also present was Minister in the Prime Minister's Department (Religious Affairs) Dr Zulkifli Hasan.
Anwar said he was prepared to take a firm position in defending the Malay rulers to ensure the constitutional monarchy continued alongside the executive branch of government.
He said he was also confident that the people, particularly Malays, as well as Chinese and Indians, would support the existing system to ensure the country's stability.
"It is not as if he has just become the Yang di-Pertuan Besar. After so many years, suddenly there is a move to remove him.
"That is the Undangs' decision, but I said, discuss it properly.
"I do not agree. You cannot simply remove a ruler. The constitutional monarchy system does not work that way.
"The ruler should not be slighted. If there is a problem or disagreement, I would seek an audience and express my views.
"You cannot remove a ruler. If a ruler can be removed so easily, the royal institution will disappear from this country," he said.

On Wednesday, Anwar described the action by Negri Sembilan Menteri Besar Datuk Ismail Lasim and the state executive council to remove Yang di-Pertuan Besar Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir as "rude" and "uncivilised".

Ismail had earlier confirmed that the proclamation to remove Tuanku Muhriz as Yang di-Pertuan Besar was unanimously decided and endorsed by the state executive council. Reports at the time said the state executive council took that position, while the Dewan Keadilan dan Undang later reiterated that Tuanku Muhriz remained the lawful Yang di-Pertuan Besar.

6d12f9240452720a: LOS ANGELES: Cities and states across the US celebrated the inaugural Dolly Parton Day on Friday - 9/25 - a date that recalls one of the late country icon's most beloved hits.
Parton died last month at the age of 80, plunging her fans into mourning for a singer-songwriter, philanthropist and businesswoman whom many saw as a unifying figure in a divided America.

This week, California governor Gavin Newsom said he was establishing the day to encourage citizens of America's most populous state to take inspiration from the "9 to 5" singer, who starred in the 1980 film of the same name with Jane Fonda and Lily Tomlin.
The movie's signature song, written and performed by Parton, has become a workplace empowerment anthem.
"We could all afford to live a little more like Dolly. Be kind, be humble, and have some fun... Be a diamond in a rhinestone world," Newsom said.

"With this bill, we are not just establishing a day to celebrate Dolly Parton, we are creating an annual reminder to us, every year, to live the way she did -- joyfully, graciously, and with a whole lot of heart."
Events around the Golden State were to include musical performances and giveaways in downtown Los Angeles.

The New York borough of Manhattan proclaimed the date to be Dolly Parton Appreciation Day, while New Orleans designated Friday as Dolly Day.

In her home state of Tennessee a number of counties proclaimed Dolly Parton Day to go alongside the state-wide recognition on her January 19 birthday.

6f6b127f14b4c006: PETALING JAYA: Perikatan Nasional’s suspension is expected to have little impact on PAS in the upcoming Melaka state election, though it may present a challenge for Hamzah Zainudin’s Wawasan, according to a political analyst.
Azmi Hassan of Akademi Nusantara said PAS was sufficiently established to contest under its own logo.
“But Wawasan is very new and unfamiliar to Melaka voters,” he told FMT, adding that the two parties would have “no choice” but to contest under their respective banners following the suspension.
The Registrar of Societies (RoS) suspended PN on Wednesday, one day after issuing a notice to show cause following a complaint lodged by Bersatu.
RoS said the suspension was intended to safeguard the organisation’s interests and did not amount to a cancellation of PN’s registration.
Azmi, however, said PN’s suspension was unlikely to derail seat negotiations between Umno and PAS, as Umno appears to have been dealing primarily with PAS rather than PN as a whole.
The development could even push PAS and Umno to conclude their negotiations sooner, he added.

On Thursday, Barisan Nasional chairman Ahmad Zahid Hamidi said PN’s components were likely to revert to contesting under their own logos in the Melaka state election as well as the next general election.
University of Tasmania analyst James Chin agreed that PN’s suspension would not impact seat negotiations between PAS and Umno.
However, Chin said the bigger question was whether PAS was able to keep PN together. PN is chaired by PAS vice-president Ahmad Samsuri Mokhtar.
“If PAS cannot get the coalition going, it will be deregistered and there'll be one less coalition in Malaysia,” he added.
International Islamic University Malaysia analyst Syaza Shukri said the suspension would put PN at a disadvantage when negotiating for seats with BN.
Prior to the suspension, there were talks that BN and PN would join forces for the Melaka state election.
“But at this stage, PN looks like it is in a mess.”
Universiti Teknologi Malaysia analyst Mazlan Ali, however, said the suspension could significantly affect PAS outside the states of Kedah, Kelantan, Terengganu and Perlis—collectively known as “SG4”.
“PAS relies on the PN brand outside the SG4 states, where the PAS symbol struggles to gain acceptance particularly among non-Malays,” he said.
The Melaka state assembly was dissolved on Wednesday, paving the way for a state election. The suspension of PN activities took effect the following day.
c53188828b0ab8f1: PETALING JAYA: Penggantungan Perikatan Nasional (PN) dijangka tidak memberi kesan besar terhadap PAS pada PRN Melaka akan datang, namun perkembangan itu mungkin mencetuskan cabaran buat Wawasan, parti pimpinan Hamzah Zainudin, menurut penganalisis politik.

“PAS bergantung pada jenama PN di luar negeri SG4, memandangkan simbol PAS sukar meraih sokongan, khususnya dalam kalangan pengundi bukan Melayu,” katanya.
DUN Melaka dibubarkan pada Rabu, sekali gus membuka laluan kepada pelaksanaan PRN, manakala penggantungan kegiatan PN berkuat kuasa pada keesokan harinya.
4838c8cafa464b49: KLUANG: At the young age of 102, Saimah Sajiman still prefers the kind of food she has enjoyed for years - simple dishes, plenty of vegetables, and meals eaten at regular hours.
Better known as Tok Saimah, the centenarian from Kampung Rahmat in Sri Lalang here has a particular fondness for boiled and steamed dishes, although she does not completely avoid other types of food.
“I prefer boiled food such as sayur bening, ikan pais and traditional village ulam,” she told Bernama at her home. "But this does not mean I don't like fried foods, too."
Born in 1924, Tok Saimah was active in gardening when she was younger and has continued to keep a steady daily routine as she has grown older.
Her mealtimes, in particular, rarely change. Breakfast is usually something light between 8am and 9am, while lunch comes before Zohor prayers and dinner before Isyak.
For her daughter, Fatimah Surip, seeing her mother remain relatively well at such an advanced age is something she does not take for granted.

Fatimah, 78, said her mum does not have any chronic illnesses, although her hearing is not as sharp as it once was. She can still stand while performing her prayers, but generally prefers using a wheelchair to move around.
“If you want to converse with her, you have to speak a little louder,” Fatimah explained.

Family life around Tok Saimah is a busy one: she has more than 20 grandchildren and 50 great-grandchildren, spanning generations that grew up in a very different Malaysia from the one she knew as a young woman.
She has lived through the Japanese occupation, British colonial rule and the communist insurgency, giving her memories that stretch across some of the country’s most turbulent periods.
And fun fact: Tok Saimah recently drew attention on social media after receiving a visit from Raja Zarith Sofiah, Queen of Malaysia, at her home!

But beyond the attention that comes with being over a century old, her days remain rooted in the same ordinary habits she has followed for decades - familiar food, regular prayers, and a routine that has long given shape to everyday life.
